By CLRN team / January 18, 2025 **How Much Does Data Annotation Pay?** **Understanding the Rewards of Data Annotation** Data annotation is a crucial step in the machine learning process, where human annotators label and categorize data to prepare it for use in AI models. The quality and accuracy of the data annotation play a significant role in the success of the machine learning model. Data annotation is the process of labeling and categorizing data to prepare it for use in machine learning models. **Pay Rates for Data Annotation** The pay rates for data annotation vary depending on the type of annotation, the complexity of the task, and the location of the annotator. Here are some approximate pay rates for data annotation: * **Text annotation**: $20-$50 per hour * **Image annotation**: $30-$70 per hour * **Audio annotation**: $25-$60 per hour The pay rates for data annotation can vary depending on several factors, including: * **Location**: Annotators in urban areas tend to earn more than those in rural areas. Data annotation also comes with several challenges, including: * **Time-consuming**: Data annotation can be a time-consuming process, requiring a high level of attention to detail and accuracy. Data annotation is a crucial step in the machine learning process, and the pay rate for data annotation can vary depending on the type of annotation, the complexity of the task, and the location of the annotator. While the pay rates for data annotation can be competitive, the challenges of the job, such as time-consuming work and limited job opportunities, can make it difficult for some individuals to succeed in this field. **Table: Pay Rates for Data Annotation** Data annotation is a rewarding field that offers a stable job opportunity, flexibility, and the chance for advancement. While the pay rates for data annotation can vary depending on the type of annotation and the location of the annotator, the benefits of the job, including job security and the opportunity for advancement, make it a worthwhile career choice for those who are passionate about data annotation. While existing works (Kocmi & Federmann, 2023; Fernandes et al., 2023; Hasanain et al., 2024; Kasner & Dušek, 2024; Chang et al., 2024; Kartáč et al., 2025; Ramponi et al., 2025; Zouhar et al., 2024) applied LLMs as a tool for evaluating their systems, our study systematically compares LLMs to human annotators across tasks and domains. We cover three span annotation tasks of different quantitative and qualitative aspects: evaluation of data-to-text generation (D2T-Eval; Section 4.1), evaluation of machine translation (MT-Eval; Section 4.2), and propaganda detection (Propaganda; Section 4.3). For our span annotator LLMs, we use a mix of open and proprietary state-of-the-art models: (1) instruction-tuned models Llama 3.3 70B Grattafiori et al. Using LLMs, as opposed to human annotators, is notably different once the financial aspect is taken into account: For D2T-Eval, crowdsourced annotation for 1k outputs costs approximately $500, while annotating the same amount of outputs with the high-performance model o3-mini LLM costs $3.60. results.title: How to Write Annotation Guidelines for Entity Extraction | Babel Street
results.content: # How to Write Annotation Guidelines for Entity Extraction. *Writing annotation guidelines for entity extraction for adverse media screening in financial compliance*. As much as we love to think our machine learning algorithms are the most important part of training up a model, they need human-annotated data to get started, which also — very importantly — are the benchmark for evaluating a model’s accuracy. Here are the steps that will take you through the process of writing annotation guidelines using the example of entity extraction:. 4. Run a pilot annotation project with a quantity of data\* (minimum of three annotators)Check for inter-annotator agreement to see where the annotators tagged text differentlyHave a meeting with the annotators to figure out what was unclear or erroneousUpdate the guidelines to address points of confusion. For more details on the annotation process, see our blog post A Day in the Life of… Building a New Entity Extraction Model.*. When you work through the inter-annotator agreement with your annotators, the question of which tagging was correct might require you to refer back to your use case, and refine the purpose your NLP will be serving. For the purpose of illustration, let’s suppose we are writing annotation guidelines for entity extraction, and that these entities will feed into a system that is detecting negative news about certain individuals or organizations — aka, adverse media screening for financial compliance. 3. Several negative examples of each type (“Do NOT annotate X in the following context:\_\_\_\_”), including non-entities and instances of ambiguity between different types. 4. Instructing annotators to tag obvious misspellings of entities, as the misspelled words are still a true signal of where a real entity would appear. Do you tag the longest entity or does your task require tagging the location and the organization within the title? The above is just a starting point for writing annotation guidelines. Ultimately, an easy-to-understand annotation guide with plentiful examples of each rule (with examples of what to tag and what not to tag) will help your human annotators produce consistently tagged data that will enable your model to become accurate and yield useful results.
